title: Gateway & Service Auth: Quick Revision Handbook
summary: Quick revision notes on securing microservices: edge authentication at the gateway, JWT and OAuth2 token propagation, service-to-service auth with mTLS, zero trust, secrets management and per-service authorization.

chapters.title: Auth Mental Model and Edge Authentication
points: Authentication (authN) proves who the caller is; authorization (authZ) decides what they may do. Return 401 for unauthenticated, 403 for authenticated but forbidden.
Edge authentication: the API gateway is the single entry point, so it validates credentials once and rejects bad traffic before it reaches services.
Gateway flow: verify token signature, issuer (iss), audience (aud), expiry (exp) and not-before (nbf), then forward the request with identity attached.
Gateway also does rate limiting, TLS termination and strips client-supplied identity headers (e.g. X-User-Id) so they cannot be spoofed.
Example: client sends 'Authorization: Bearer <JWT>' to the gateway, which validates it against the IdP's JWKS endpoint (keys cached, refreshed on unknown kid).

chapters.title: JWT and OAuth2 Token Propagation
points: JWT = header.payload.signature, base64url-encoded. The payload is signed, NOT encrypted, so never put secrets in claims.
Key claims: sub (subject), iss (issuer), aud (audience), exp (expiry), iat (issued at), scope/roles. Short-lived access tokens (5-15 min) plus refresh tokens.
Signing: HS256 uses one shared secret; RS256/ES256 use a private key to sign and a public key (JWKS) to verify, so services verify without being able to mint tokens.
OAuth2 flows: Authorization Code + PKCE for users and SPAs; Client Credentials for machine-to-machine; avoid Implicit and Password flows.
Propagation: forward the user's token downstream to preserve identity, or use Token Exchange (RFC 8693) to get a narrower, audience-restricted token per hop (avoids the confused deputy problem).
Opaque token vs JWT: opaque requires introspection (RFC 7662) call to the IdP, so it is revocable instantly; JWT is verified locally but hard to revoke before exp.
Mistakes: accepting alg=none, not checking aud/iss, trusting an unverified decoded token, long-lived tokens, storing tokens in localStorage.

chapters.title: Service-to-Service Auth and mTLS
points: Services must authenticate each other; a private network is not proof of identity. Options: mTLS, service JWT via Client Credentials, or both.
mTLS: both client and server present X.509 certificates in the TLS handshake, each verifying the other against a trusted CA. One-way TLS only authenticates the server.
Service identity lives in the certificate, e.g. a SPIFFE ID like spiffe://prod/ns/payments/sa/api, issued by SPIRE or the mesh CA.

Service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) sidecars handle mTLS transparently with automatic short-lived cert issuance and rotation; Istio PeerAuthentication mode STRICT rejects plaintext traffic, PERMISSIVE allows both during migration.
mTLS proves which service is calling (workload identity); a JWT proves which user it acts for. Production systems usually use both.
Mistakes: long-lived certs with no rotation, leaving mesh on PERMISSIVE forever, skipping cert chain/expiry checks.

chapters.title: Zero Trust and Secrets Management
points: Zero trust: never trust based on network location; authenticate and authorize every request, assume breach, grant least privilege.
Zero trust building blocks: strong workload identity, mTLS everywhere, per-request policy checks, network segmentation (default-deny NetworkPolicy), continuous logging.
Secrets (DB passwords, API keys, private keys) belong in a secrets manager such as HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager or Kubernetes Secrets with encryption at rest, never in code, images or Git.
Prefer dynamic secrets: Vault issues short-lived DB credentials per service with a TTL and lease, auto-revoked on expiry, instead of static shared passwords.
Services fetch secrets at runtime using their workload identity (IAM role, K8s service account); rotate regularly and never log secrets.
Mistakes: secrets in env vars baked into images, one shared secret for all services, committing .env files, no rotation plan; note K8s Secrets are only base64-encoded by default.

chapters.title: Authorization Per Service
points: Gateway checks coarse authN and basic scopes; each service must enforce its own fine-grained authZ (defense in depth), because the gateway can be bypassed or misconfigured.

Models: RBAC (roles like admin/editor), ABAC (attributes such as owner, region, time), ReBAC (relationships, e.g. Zanzibar-style); scopes limit what a client app can do, roles limit what a user can do.
Check object-level ownership in the service (user can only read their own order) to prevent BOLA/IDOR, the top API vulnerability.
Externalize policy with OPA (Rego) or Cedar as a sidecar or library so rules are versioned and consistent; decision = allow/deny per request on input of subject, action, resource.
Example: Order service verifies the JWT aud='orders', requires scope 'orders:read', then checks order.owner_id == token.sub before returning data.
Mistakes: relying only on the gateway, trusting identity headers from callers, authorizing by scope but not by resource owner, hard-coding role checks across services.

chapters.title: Gateway Auth Cheat Sheet
points: Status codes: 401 = not authenticated, 403 = not allowed, 429 = rate limited.
JWT validation checklist: signature, alg allow-list, iss, aud, exp/nbf, then claims for authZ.
Flows: Auth Code + PKCE (users), Client Credentials (services), Token Exchange (downstream narrowing).
mTLS = both sides present certs; mesh STRICT mode enforces it; SPIFFE ID names the workload.
Secrets: manager + dynamic short-lived creds + rotation; never in Git or images.
Authorization: gateway coarse, service fine-grained, always check resource ownership; policy via OPA/Cedar.
